title: Accessible Communication & Digital Content
summary: Learn how clear communication, captions, transcripts, alt text, readable documents, and accessible digital practices can reduce unnecessary workplace barriers.
objectives: Identify common accessibility features used in workplace communication and digital content.
Explain why important information should not depend on only one sensory or interaction method.
Recognize basic ways to make workplace communication clearer and more accessible.

vocab.def: Text that represents spoken dialogue and other important audio information.
A text version of spoken or recorded content.
A text description that communicates the purpose or important information of an image.
The ability to operate a digital interface without requiring a mouse or touch input.

sections.heading: Important information should be perceivable
sections.body: When information is only spoken, only visual, or only available through one interaction method, some people may be excluded. Multiple accessible representations can reduce that barrier.

sections.heading: Captions and transcripts provide another path
sections.body: Captions and transcripts can help people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, people in noisy environments, people learning terminology, and others who benefit from text.

sections.heading: Images need meaningful alternatives when they carry information
sections.body: If an image, chart, or diagram communicates important information, an accessible text description can help make that information available to people who cannot perceive the visual content directly.

sections.heading: Accessible interaction matters too
sections.body: Digital content should not depend unnecessarily on precise mouse movement, color alone, rapid motion, or other interaction patterns that can create barriers.

practice.prompt: A required training video explains emergency procedures but has no captions or transcript. What accessibility concern exists?
practice.answer: Important information is available only through audio, which can create a barrier for people who cannot access it effectively.

practice.prompt: A chart uses red and green with no labels to show pass and fail. What is a stronger approach?
practice.answer: Add text labels, symbols, or other non-color information so meaning does not depend on color alone.

quiz.question: What is the strongest accessibility principle for workplace information?
options: Provide important information in ways that do not depend unnecessarily on one sensory or interaction method
Assume everyone can use the same device in the same way
quiz.answer: Provide important information in ways that do not depend unnecessarily on one sensory or interaction method

lab.objective: Review simulated workplace emails, documents, videos, forms, and presentations and identify simple accessibility improvements.

reflectionPrompt: Which accessibility feature could improve communication for people beyond the group it was originally designed to support?
